scores.reason: Peter commanding the lame man at the Beautiful Gate with John beside him in mid-afternoon matches the verse and the ninth-hour context; the onlookers are generic.
Jesus arriving at Jairus's house and seeing the wailing mourners, with Peter, James and John behind him, is faithful to the verse; the composition is coherent.
Saul entering Jerusalem with Barnabas and the apostles is a faithful, coherent rendering of the verse.
Abraham and Ishmael undergoing circumcision on the same day, restrained and non-graphic in the camp, is a faithful representative image of the verse.
Jesus quoting the psalm while teaching in the temple courts, with disciples, scribes and crowd, is faithful and coherent.
A generic deceiver feigning innocence before a doubtful neighbour is a faithful representative scene of the proverb; the author is correctly left out.
The four living creatures' straight legs and burnished-bronze feet beside the Chebar, with the divine presence only as storm-cloud light, is faithful; Ezekiel is correctly left out.
The exchange between Jesus and James and John is rendered faithfully, but the setting depicts Jericho, an available cast entry that is not selected.

defects.quote: Dusty road outside Jericho with stone walls and palm trees in the distance
defects.reason: Depicts the Jericho location (walls and palms), a cast entry missing from selected; in Mark the group reaches Jericho only at 10:46.

scores.reason: Solomon, the author of the proverb, is placed in the illustrative scene as a seated listener.

defects.quote: Solomon seated calmly to one side, listening with a steady gaze
defects.reason: Framing figure: the proverb's author is shown as a participant in the scene that illustrates his saying.

defects.quote: Solomon framed in the background pillars
defects.reason: Repeats the framing-figure placement in the composition.

scores.reason: Jesus teaching love of enemies to a crowd near Galilee is a faithful scene (a hillside rise slightly conflates Luke's 'level place' but stays within reason).
God's veiled white-gold light, which matches the unselected hasForm:false entry's canon, is added to the ruined street even though nothing in the verse calls for it.

defects.quote: a distant veiled light of white-gold behind dense slow cloud
defects.reason: Depicts God's presence (an available cast entry that is not selected) and nearly restates that entry's canon of white-gold light veiled by dense slow cloud.

defects.quote: with the veiled light of cloud receding in the background
defects.reason: Repeats the unselected divine-presence effect in the composition.

scores.reason: The beloved's hand through the latch at night while the robe-less Shulammite reacts inside is faithful and coherent; showing only the hand is a good choice.
A representative father-and-son scene in a Judean village suits a genealogy verse that has no cast.
Moses and Aaron counting the Levite families by the tabernacle, with God shown only as cloud-radiance, is faithful to the verse.
Paul, who writes the request for prayer from elsewhere, is shown in person at Thessalonica leading the believers.

defects.quote: Paul standing near the front, arms slightly raised, facing the gathered believers
defects.reason: Framing figure: the letter's author is placed among the recipients as if he made the request in person in Thessalonica, which the epistolary source contradicts.

scores.reason: Moses is recast as the officiating priest performing a Sabbath burnt offering that the verse only commands the priests to make.

defects.quote: Moses in priestly linen beside the bronze altar, with two young lambs held forward
defects.reason: Moses relays the law and is not a priest; dressing him in priestly linen to perform the future Sabbath offering gives him an identity and role the source does not support.

defects.quote: Moses lifts a hand toward the presented lambs, readying them for the Sabbath burnt offering
defects.reason: Shows the law-giver officiating at the offering instead of the priests.

scores.reason: Jesus quoting the psalm to disciples and crowd in the temple court is faithful and coherent.
The righteous gathered under breaking light, with God implied only as radiance, is a faithful symbolic image for the psalm verse.
God is still commanding the altar here, yet the scene shows the linen court already standing and has Moses laying out the altar on Horeb's slope; it also restates God's canon almost word for word.

defects.quote: with a sacred camp of hanging linen visible below
defects.reason: The linen-hung court of the sanctuary is only being commanded in this section (Exod 27:9-19) and does not exist yet.

defects.quote: a brilliant white-gold radiance veiled by slowly moving cloud, fire-like glow at its heart
defects.reason: Restates the fixed canon of the hasForm:false God entry nearly verbatim.

scores.reason: Gebim's villagers fleeing along a Judean hill road is a faithful, coherent image of the verse.
Israelite families eating unleavened bread by the tabernacle with Moses present is a faithful representative scene for the feast law.
The ash-gathering itself is faithful, but two details are doubtful, so a reasonable reader could go either way.

defects.quote: a cedar, hyssop and scarlet thread bundle set aside
defects.reason: Numbers 19:6 has the cedar, hyssop and scarlet cast into the burning heifer, so they should already be consumed when the ashes are gathered.

defects.quote: the veiled cloud high above Horeb
defects.reason: The phrasing may introduce the unselected divine presence, though Horeb's own cloud-wrapped summit may explain it.

scores.reason: The guide measuring the south gate with Ezekiel led along is faithful, but two details are doubtful, so a reasonable reader could go either way.

defects.quote: a faint veiled cloud-glow at the edge of the scene
defects.reason: This may depict the unselected divine presence, whose glory returns to the temple only in Ezekiel 43.

defects.quote: Stone gateway of a vast inner temple court
defects.reason: The south gate measured in 40:24 belongs to the outer court; the inner court's south gate comes at 40:27-28.

scores.reason: Pharaoh receiving the news in his palace and recoiling with his servants is faithful to the verse.
A righteous man giving to a widow while a wicked rich man seethes is a faithful representative contrast for the proverb.
The verse is Belshazzar speaking to Daniel, but the plan makes the queen the speaker recalling Daniel's reputation, which happened earlier (5:10-12).

defects.quote: She is speaking, gesturing gently as she recalls Daniel's reputation to the court.
defects.reason: Wrong speaker and instant: in 5:13-14 the king addresses Daniel; the queen's speech came before Daniel was brought in.

defects.quote: The queen in court robes, half-turned toward Daniel with a composed, attentive expression.
defects.reason: Makes the queen the primary subject of a verse spoken by the king.

scores.reason: Jeremiah, the prophet delivering the oracle against idols, is placed inside the goldsmith's workshop that the oracle describes.

defects.quote: Jeremiah standing quietly in the doorway in plain mourning cloak
defects.reason: Framing figure: the prophet who speaks the oracle is shown as a participant in the scene it describes.

defects.quote: Jeremiah at the edge of the frame
defects.reason: Repeats the framing figure in the composition.

scores.reason: Jeremiah delivering the word about iron bars to Hananiah in the temple court, with the broken yoke as context, is a faithful representative scene.
A named individual, Aaron, is substituted for the generic 'the priest' of this case law.

defects.quote: Aaron in priestly linen, holding a clay cup of water toward the woman
defects.reason: The ordeal law names only a generic 'the priest'; casting Aaron replaces the generic role with a named person.

scores.reason: Jeremiah preaching in the temple court while the people turn stiff-necked away fits the temple sermon and 7:27's 'they will not listen to you'.
